The appendix proof of Theorem 11 runs over a section and three subsections, so it is emitted as one proof node per part (PP29, PP30, PP32, PP33). Each part has a proves edge to TP6 and a continuation edge to the main-text pointer PP9.

nodes.name: ORM-adaptive systems
nodes.statement: We denote the underlying open--loop systems in all these cases as {\em Open-loop Reference Model} (ORM)--adaptive systems.

nodes.name: Combined/composite direct and indirect Model Reference Adaptive Control (CMRAC)
nodes.statement: Another class of adaptive systems that have been explored in the past where a noticeable improvement in transient performance was obtained is in the context of {\em Combined/composite direct and indirect Model Reference Adaptive Control} (CMRAC) \cite{duarte1989combined,slotine1989composite}.
nodes.definiendum: Combined/composite direct and indirect Model Reference Adaptive Control (CMRAC)
nodes.statement_short: CMRAC: adaptive systems combining direct and indirect adaptation, known for improved transients.

nodes.name: CMRAC with Closed-loop reference models (CMRAC-C)
nodes.statement: The resulting {\em CMRAC with Closed-loop reference models} (CMRAC-C) are shown to be stable, enable the feedback of noise-free state estimates while guaranteeing stability, and most importantly are shown to have guaranteed transient properties.

nodes.name: Plant with scalar input
nodes.statement: Consider the linear system dynamics with scalar input \begin{equation} \dot x(t) = A_p x(t) + b u(t) \end{equation} where ${x(t) \in \mathbb R^n}$ is the state vector, ${u(t)\in \mathbb R}$ is the control input, ${A_p\in \mathbb R^{n \times n}}$ is unknown and ${b\in \mathbb R^n}$ is known.
nodes.statement_short: Linear plant with unknown state matrix $A_p$ and known input vector $b$.

nodes.name: Plant dynamics
nodes.statement: \dot x(t) = A_p x(t) + b u(t)
nodes.label: s1:sys

nodes.name: Reference model state
nodes.statement: Our goal is to design the control input such that ${x(t)}$ follows the reference model state ${x_m(t)\in \mathbb R^n}$ defined by the following dynamics \begin{equation} \dot x_m(t) = A_m x_m(t) + b r(t) - L(x(t)-x_m(t)) \end{equation} where ${A_m \in \mathbb R^{n\times n }}$ is Hurwtitz and ${r(t)\in \mathbb R}$ is a bounded possible time varying reference command.
nodes.statement_short: Reference model state $x_m$ driven by Hurwitz $A_m$, bounded command $r$ and feedback $-L(x-x_m)$.

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference model (CRM)
nodes.statement: \dot x_m(t) = A_m x_m(t) + b r(t) - L(x(t)-x_m(t))
nodes.label: s1:ref

nodes.name: Luenberger gain
nodes.statement: ${L\in \mathbb R^{n\times n}}$ is denoted as the {\em Luenberger--gain}, and is chosen such that \begin{equation} \bar A_m \triangleq A_m+L \end{equation} is Hurwitz.
nodes.statement_short: $L$ is the Luenberger gain, chosen so that $\bar A_m = A_m+L$ is Hurwitz.

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference matrix
nodes.statement: \bar A_m \triangleq A_m+L
nodes.label: s1:ambar

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference model (CRM)
nodes.statement: Equation \eqref{s1:ref} is referred to as a CRM, and when ${L=0}$ the classical ORM is recovered.
nodes.origin_citation: Lavretsky et al.; Stepanyan & Krishnakumar (lav10aiaa, ste10)

nodes.name: Matching condition
nodes.statement: A parameter vector ${\theta^*\in\mathbb R^n}$ exists that satisfies the {\em matching condition} \begin{equation} A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: There is $\theta^*$ with $A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}$.
nodes.label: asm:m

nodes.name: Matching condition
nodes.statement: A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}.
nodes.label: s1:match

nodes.name: CRM adaptive control law and update law
nodes.statement: The control input is chosen in the form \begin{equation} u(t)= \theta^T(t) x(t) + r(t) \end{equation} where $\theta(t) \in \mathbb R^n$ is the adaptive control gain with the update law \begin{equation} \dot \theta(t) = -\Gamma x(t)e^T(t) Pb \end{equation} with ${\Gamma = \Gamma^T>0}$, ${e(t)= x(t)-x_m(t)}$ is the model following error and $P=P^T>0$ is the solution to the algebraic Lyapunov equation \begin{equation} \bar A_m^TP+P \bar A_m = -I_{n\times n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Control $u=\theta^T x + r$ with gradient update law driven by $e=x-x_m$ and $P$ solving the Lyapunov equation.

nodes.name: Control law
nodes.statement: u(t)= \theta^T(t) x(t) + r(t)
nodes.label: s1:u

nodes.name: Adaptive update law
nodes.statement: \dot \theta(t) = -\Gamma x(t)e^T(t) Pb
nodes.label: s1:law

nodes.name: Algebraic Lyapunov equation
nodes.statement: \bar A_m^TP+P \bar A_m = -I_{n\times n}.
nodes.label: s1:lyap

nodes.name: Error model and parameter error
nodes.statement: The underlying error model in this case is given by \begin{equation}\dot e(t)= \bar A_m e(t) + b \tilde\theta(t)x(t) \end{equation} where ${\tilde\theta(t)=\theta(t)-\theta^*}$ is the parameter error.

nodes.name: Error model
nodes.statement: \dot e(t)= \bar A_m e(t) + b \tilde\theta(t)x(t)
nodes.label: s1:et

nodes.name: Global stability of the CRM-adaptive system
nodes.statement: The closed-loop adaptive system with \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u} and \eqref{s1:law} is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically, under the matching condition in \eqref{s1:match}.
nodes.statement_short: Under matching, the CRM adaptive system is globally stable and the model-following error tends to zero.
assumptions: The closed-loop adaptive system with \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u} and \eqref{s1:law}
conclusions: is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically
nodes.label: thm:simple

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: It is straight forward to show using \eqref{s1:law} and \eqref{s1:et} that \begin{equation} V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta \end{equation} is a Lyapunov function. Since $e$ is bounded, the structure of \eqref{s1:ref} implies that $x_m$ is bounded. $x$ in turn and $u$ are bounded. Barbalat lemma ensures asymptotic convergence of $e(t)$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Lyapunov function $V=e^TPe+\tilde\theta^T\Gamma^{-1}\tilde\theta$ gives boundedness; Barbalat's lemma gives $e\to0$.

nodes.name: Lyapunov function V(e, theta tilde)
nodes.statement: V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta
nodes.label: can

nodes.name: Finite convergence time T(epsilon, L)
nodes.statement: For all $\epsilon>0$ there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norm{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: For every $\epsilon$ the error eventually stays within $\epsilon$ after a time $T(\epsilon,L)$.
conclusions: there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norm{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$
nodes.label: Tdef

nodes.name: CRM-adaptive system
nodes.statement: The overall CRM--adaptive system is defined by \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u}, and \eqref{s1:law}.

nodes.name: Open-loop reference model and tracking error
nodes.statement: The standard open-loop reference model is given by \begin{equation}\dot x_m^o(t) = A_m x_m^o(t) + b r(t) \end{equation} with the corresponding tracking error \begin{equation} e^o(t) = x(t) - x_m^o(t) . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Open-loop reference model (ORM)
nodes.statement: \dot x_m^o(t) = A_m x_m^o(t) + b r(t)
nodes.label: eo

nodes.name: True tracking error
nodes.statement: e^o(t) = x(t) - x_m^o(t) .
nodes.label: eodef

nodes.name: True tracking error
nodes.statement: One can in fact view the error $e^o$ as the {\em true tracking error} and $e$ as a pseudo--tracking error.

nodes.name: Convergence to the open-loop reference model
nodes.statement: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The plant state converges to the open-loop reference trajectory $x_m^o$.
conclusions: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm:simple} we can conclude that $e(t)\rightarrow0$ asymptotically. Thus we can conclude that $x_m(t) \rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $e(t)\rightarrow 0$, implying that $e^o\rightarrow 0$, thus $x(t)\rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: $e\to0$ from Theorem 1 forces $x_m\to x_m^o$, hence $x\to x_m^o$.

nodes.name: CRM as a nonlinear reference model
nodes.statement: The choice of the CRM as in (2) essentially makes the reference model nonlinear, as $x$ depends on $\theta$ which in turn depends on $x_m$ in a highly nonlinear manner. In general, the tracking problem in a ORM--adaptive system can be viewed as one where an overall nonlinear time-varying system is to be designed such that its output tracks that of a linear time-invariant system. The CRM-adaptive system is one where the overall nonlinear system is instead required to follow a nonlinear (reference) model. This nonlinear model, however, is chosen such that it asymptotically approaches the original linear reference model in the classical case, and hence the CRM-adaptive system retains all the desired characteristics of the ORM-adaptive system. As we will show in Section \ref{section:perf}, the CRM-adaptive system has an additional desirable property, of quantifiable transient properties, which the ORM-adaptive system may not necessarily possess. We will also show in this section that this is made possible by virtue of the additional degree of freedom available to the adaptive system in the form of the feedback gain in the CRM.
nodes.statement_short: The CRM makes the reference model nonlinear but asymptotically equal to the linear one, adding quantifiable transients.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: $A_m$ is Hurwitz and therefore $\sigma>0$. It is not necessary however that the sum $A_m+A_m^T$ is Hurwitz. The trace operator is denoted as $\text{Tr} (\cdot)$ and is a linear operator. Recalling that a matrix and its transpose have the same trace we can conclude that $\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m) =\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m+A_m^T)/2$. Finally we have that \begin{equation*} s \geq -\frac 1 {2n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right) = -\frac 1 n \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(A_m) \geq \sigma>0. \ \IEEEQEDopen \end{equation*} \let\IEEEQED\relax
nodes.statement_short: Trace argument: average eigenvalue of the symmetric part equals that of $A_m$, bounded by $-\sigma$.

assumptions: $A_m$ Hurwitz with constants $\sigma$ and $a$ as defined in \eqref{s1:ambound}

nodes.name: Projection-based adaptive law
nodes.statement: The projection based adaptive law, which replaces \eqref{s1:law}, is given by \begin{equation} \dot \theta(t) = \text{Proj}_\Gamma \left(\theta(t),-x e^T P b ,f \right) \end{equation} where the $\Gamma$--projection function, $\text{Proj}_\Gamma$, is defined as in Appendix \ref{ap:proj} and $f$ is a convex function given by \begin{equation} f(\theta;\vartheta,\varepsilon) = \frac{\norm \theta^2 -\vartheta^2}{2 \varepsilon \vartheta - \varepsilon^2} \end{equation} where $\vartheta$ and $\varepsilon$ are positive constants chosen as $\vartheta = \theta^*_\text{max}$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Free design parameters ell and ell/gamma
nodes.statement: In this section it is argued that the free design parameters for the adaptive system are $\ell$ and the ratio of $\ell$ and $\gamma$. It is clear from \eqref{V_1} that the rate of exponential decay of the Lyapunov function is solely a function of the slowest eigenvalue of $\sigma$ and $\ell$. The term $\sigma$ is defined by the open--loop reference model jacobiam $A_m$ in \eqref{s1:ref} and cannot be independently increased without also increasing the bound on $\theta^*$, due to the fact that $A_m= A_p+b\theta^{*T}$ from \eqref{s1:match}. Therfore, from \eqref{alpha1} it is clear that while increasing $\sigma$ increases $\alpha_1$ it also increases the size of of the compact set $\mathcal E$ that the model following error is exponentially converging to. The Luenberger gain $\ell$, in contrast, does not affect the matching condition for the adaptive system and therefore increasing $\ell$ does not result in a high--gain matching condition. It is seen from \eqref{b1} that while increasing $\ell$ may result in a larger $\alpha_1$ which is desirable, it also increases the $\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1$. At first glance this seems undesirable. However, it is important to note that $\ell$ is inversely proportional to the bounds for $P$ in \eqref{s1:pbound} and \eqref{minP}. Upon further inspection of the tuning law in \eqref{s2:adaplaw}, when Projeciton is not active the adaptive law reduces to \begin{equation*} \dot\theta= -\gamma x e^T P b, \end{equation*} and therefore, the only fixed parameters that control the rate of adaptation are $\gamma, P(\ell)$ and $b$. Given that $b$ is fixed it is ignored and thus the learning rate is a function of $\gamma \norm P $. Therefore, if $\gamma$ and $\ell$ are increased at the same rate, the effective rate of change in the adaptive tuning law will remain the same, which illustrates that the ratio of $\ell$ and $\gamma$ is an important design parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Argues $\ell$ and the ratio $\gamma/\ell$ are the free design parameters since the learning rate scales with $\gamma\|P\|$.

nodes.statement: The bounds on $e(t)$ and the $\mathcal L_2$--norm of $\dot\theta$ directly show that CRM--adaptive systems lead to smaller $e(t)$ than with the ORM which are obtained by setting $\ell=0$ in \eqref{e2e} and \eqref{el2}. This indicates that there is a trade-off between fast transients and true tracking error. The signal that succinctly captures this trade off is $\dot u$, whose behavior is captured in detail using the time intervals $\mathbb T1$, $\mathbb T2$, and $\mathbb T3$. We also showed in Theorem \ref{thmpopt} that this trade-off can be optimized via a suitable choice of $\ell$ and $\rho$. In what follows, we compare this optimized CRM with ORM and show that the former is clearly better than the latter.

nodes.name: Comparison of CRM and ORM control-rate bounds
nodes.statement: We now compare the bounds on $\dot u$ using observations (A1)--(A3) and (B1)--(B3). In order to have the same basis for comparison, we assume that $\gamma$, $\sigma$, and $\ell$ are such that $\rho=\rho_0$ and that both CRM-- and ORM--adaptive systems start with the same bound at $t=0$. As noted above, a tight bound cannot be derived for the ORM-based adaptive system over $[N\tau_1^*,N\tau_2^\prime)$. In the best scenario, one can assume that this bound is no larger than that over $[0,N\tau_1^*]$. This allows us to derive the bounds shown in Figure \ref{fig:udot}. The main observations that one can make from this figure are summarized below: \begin{itemize} \item Even though at time $t = 0$, both the ORM and CRM have the same bound, since $\tau_1$ can be made much smaller than $\tau_2^\prime$, this bound is valid for a much shorter time with the CRM-system than in the ORM--system. This helps us conclude that the initial transients can be made to subside much faster in the former case than the latter, by suitably choosing $\ell$. \item The bound on $\dot u$ for $\mathbb T_2$ with the CRM--adaptive system is however linear in powers of $\ell$ and hence can be larger than the bound on $\dot u$ with the ORM-adaptive system over $\mathbb T_2^\prime$. \item The above observations clearly illustrate, if the cost function $U(N\tau_2^\prime;\rho,\ell)$ is minimized then the CRM system will have smoother transients than the ORM. Then, at larger times the error dynamics will asymptotically converges to zero. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Effect of disturbance and time variation on the compact set
nodes.statement: From the above Theorem it is is shown that in the presence of disturbance and time--varying uncertainty, the rate of exponential decay of the lyapunov function is $\alpha_1/2$ where $\alpha_1$ was the rate of exponential decay for the system with constant uncertainty and no disturbances. The term that controls how the compact set $\mathcal E$ grows with the upper bound on the rate of change of the time-varying matched uncertainty is $\beta_2$ which is inversely proportional to $\gamma$. $\beta_3$ scales the size of the compact set in regard to the disturbance term $d$. Therefore, increasing $\gamma$ and $\ell$ in proportion so that $\rho$ is constant constant decreases the size of the compact set $\mathcal E$.

nodes.name: Simulation: scalar time-varying plant with disturbance
nodes.statement: For this study a scalar time varying system of the form in \eqref{s2:sys} is controlled where \begin{equation*} A_p(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & 0 \leq t < 20 \\ 1+\frac{1}{4} (t-20) & 20 \leq t <24 \\ 2 & t \geq 24 \end{cases}, \end{equation*} $b=1$, and $d(t)$ is a deterministic signal used to represent a disturbance. Over the first 20 seconds $d(t)=0$. After 20 seconds $d(t)$ is generated from a Gausian distribution centered at 0 with a variance of 1, covariance of 0.1, deterministically sampled at 10 Hz with a fixed seed, and then passed through a saturation function with upper and lowers bounds of 0.2 and -0.2 respectively. nodes.statement: While the above analysis does not directly support the observed transient improvements with CMRAC, we provide a few speculations below: The free design parameter $L_i$ in the identifier is typically chosen to have eigenvalues faster than the plant that is being controlled. Therefore the identification model following error $e_i$ converges rapidly and $\hat\theta(t)$ will have smooth transients. It can be argued that the desirable transient properties of the identifier pass on to the direct component through the tuning law, and in particular $\epsilon_\theta$.
